home_company_intro: Based in Vancouver, Iceberg Dry Ice opened in 2003 and has expanded throughout BC and Alberta.
home_delivery_description: We deliver hundreds of tons of dry ice every year to both commercial and private customers.
home_distribution_info: From restoration companies to large distribution centers we distribute thousands of pounds on time every week.
home_experience_description: Over the years we"ve met some amazing people and seen some fantastic projects come to life.
home_applications_description: Houses transform into spooky graveyards for Halloween, cocktail parties have a little extra pizazz with smoking drinks, birthday party cakes become works of art with erupting volcanoes and camping trips never end in soggy messes from melted wet ice.
dryice_uses.smoke_effects.title: Smoke Effects
dryice_uses.smoke_effects.intro: Dry Ice can be used to create a very effective thick, ground-hugging fog great for parties, dance floors, boiling cauldrons, fancy drinks and more. When dry ice warms up it cools the surrounding air and causes water vapor to condense, forming a cool white mist that sinks to the ground and stays there.
dryice_uses.smoke_effects.tips: If you put dry ice in a bowl of water this effect is multiplied many times over. Depending on the effect you want you'll need different amounts of dry ice as seen below.
dryice_uses.punch_bowls.title: Punch Bowls
dryice_uses.punch_bowls.description: Punch bowls are the easiest effects to make. Just drop some dry ice in water and it will bubble and boil and make smoke. Use a perforated container so you don't accidentally serve dry ice in drinks.
dryice_uses.cauldrons.title: Cauldrons
dryice_uses.cauldrons.description: Making a bubbling witches cauldron is similar to a punch bowl, but uses more dry ice and more water to encourage overflow. Check out this display made by Creative Eye Media.
dryice_uses.dance_floors.title: Dance Floors and Graveyards
dryice_uses.dance_floors.description: To cover the ground with flowing smoke that billows out, you can use several methods:
dryice_uses.dance_floors.option1: Multiple Cauldrons: Use several cauldrons filled with dry ice to pump smoke from different spots.
dryice_uses.dance_floors.option2: Dry Ice Smoke Machine: Rent a machine like a Pea Souper that lowers dry ice into heated water.
dryice_uses.dance_floors.option3: Smoke Machine + Dry Ice: Run chemical smoke through a dry ice container to cool it. Best for static setups, not active dance floors.
dryice_uses.dance_floors.note: For videos showing smoke over time, check our videos below.
dryice_uses.food_storage.title: Food Storage
dryice_uses.food_storage.description1: Dry ice is great for food storage. It lasts 5x longer than regular ice and doesn’t leave water behind.
dryice_uses.food_storage.description2: Freeze food first, and use ice packs or gel packs to extend freshness. Separate dry ice with newspaper to prevent freezer burn.
dryice_uses.science.title: Science!
dryice_uses.science.text1: Dry ice is perfect for science experiments or fun food displays like volcano cakes!
dryice_uses.science.text2: Watch how soap and dry ice combine to make fun water vapor effects.
dryice_uses.science.video_credit: Note: This video was made by www.youtube.com/brusspup
dryice_uses.videos.title: Videos
dryice_uses.videos.intro: This video shows how combining dry ice and smoke machines makes low-lying fog. Cold air keeps fog close to the ground.
dryice_uses.videos.subsection: Smoke Effects - Examples - 2 lbs from 0 - 20 minutes
dryice_uses.videos.explanation: These videos help you estimate how much dry ice to use. Strong effects last ~10 minutes; dry ice is mostly gone by 20 minutes.
dryice_safety.body.1: Dry Ice is -78.5°C (-109.3°F) when in its solid form. Direct contact with carbon dioxide should be avoided as it can easily cause severe cold burns and frostbite. Think about it like the opposite of fire — don't touch it any longer than you'd stick your finger in a flame.
dryice_safety.note.1: Dry ice should always be handled with thick gloves.
dryice_safety.body.2: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide (CO₂), the gas you exhale. Carbon dioxide isn't toxic in small amounts, but in high concentrations, it displaces oxygen, making it impossible to breathe. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, headaches, and confusion. CO₂ is heavier than air and sinks to the ground, so always ventilate from ground level.
dryice_safety.title.3: Dry Ice Expands as it Warms Up
dryice_safety.body.3: Dry ice sublimates when it warms up, changing directly from a solid to a gas without passing through a liquid phase. It expands by a factor of 600, which can rapidly build up pressure in a sealed container.
dryice_safety.note.3: Never store dry ice in an airtight container.

blasting_info.intro.comparison: There are several different types of media that can be used to blast clean surfaces. Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. This table shows a handful of criteria for comparison which are explained in more depth below. At Iceberg Dry Ice we want you to use the right tool for the right job and when a different media would be more effective for your job we are happy to help find you the right solution.
blasting_info.sections.media.title: Media
blasting_info.sections.media.text: This is what type of media you are propelling at your cleaning surface. Silica sand can't be used anymore because it has been deemed carcinogenic by WorkSafe BC.
blasting_info.sections.mose.title: Mose
blasting_info.sections.mose.text: The Mose scale is used to rate hardness with talc being a 1, and diamonds being a 10. The harder the media the more aggressive it is in cleaning and the more damage it does to your surface. Hard media like glass and coal slag can pit metals and will destroy wood but because of this they can clean rust or do cement finishing. Softer media like dry ice and soda won't affect cement, but they can be used on wood finishing, or circuit boards safely.
blasting_info.sections.fryability.text: Fryability is a measure of how easily the media breaks apart. Dry ice and soda are highly fryable which means that instead of causing damage to your surfaces, they disintegrate on contact. This is why they are referred to as no-touch or non-aggressive cleaning techniques, and why they are used to restore masonry and clean wooden structures without impacting their structure.
blasting_info.sections.cleanup.title: Clean Up
blasting_info.sections.cleanup.text: Assuming 6.5 hours of trigger time in a standard day how much media will be lying around on the ground? Medium and hard medias are consumed at a rate of 5-6 lbs. every minute, dry ice at about 3 lbs. every minute, and soda at about 1.5 lbs. every minute. Dry ice sublimates (changes directly from a solid physical state to a gas) and disappears, leaving nothing to clean up but the contaminant you've removed. This is a very large factor to consider as it takes a lot of time to clean up the resulting media, and it may have to be disposed of if the contaminant is dangerous.
blasting_info.sections.advantages.title: Advantages

blasting_info.sections.advantages.text.cold: Cold - dry ice is -78.5°C, and sticky substances like glue, tar, ink etc. are cleaned very effectively because the contaminant is frozen and then chips off!
blasting_info.sections.advantages.text.thermalShock: Thermal Shock - dry ice will cause the surface and contaminant to change temperature at different rates causing a micro-thermal shock. This helps to pull them apart so cleaning is more effective.
blasting_info.sections.advantages.text.ecoFriendly: Environmentally Friendly - dry ice is made from recycled carbon dioxide and exists naturally in the atmosphere. Because of this it is a very green solution!
blasting_info.sections.advantages.text.soda: Buffers Smoke Smell - soda works as a strong buffer for acids and bases, because of this the smell of smoke is greatly reduced in fire restoration work.
blasting_info.sections.advantages.text.cheap: Inexpensive - power washing saves money as no specialized media is needed

blasting_info.sections.disadvantages.tex.oxygen: Oxygen Displacement - dry ice is made from carbon dioxide which will displace oxygen at a rate of ~800 cubic feet per hour. As a result, additional PPE is required if the work is being done in an enclosed space.
blasting_info.sections.disadvantages.tex.mould: Mould - the water from power washing can cause mould issues if used indoors.
blasting_info.sections.disadvantages.tex.conductive: Conductive - water is electrically conductive unlike other blasting media.
blasting_info.sections.disadvantages.tex.toxic: Environmentally UNfriendly - solvents can be very toxic which is a great reason to use dry ice blasting instead.

blasting_info.sections.how.text: Dry ice blasting is similar to power washing or sand blasting except it uses dry ice instead of water or sand respectively. When the ice hits the cleaning surface several things happen.

1. The dry ice particles immediately sublimate on contact by sucking some heat from the target. The surface cools slightly causing a small pressure wave that helps lift the dirt off like a spatula. This is called a micro-thermal shock.

2. When dry ice sublimates it expands from a solid to a gas taking up 600x as much volume. As you blast, the dry ice slips under the surface layer of dirt and then expands, causing a tremendous lifting force that cleans your target.
3. Because dry ice is extremely cold ( -78.5°C ) it proves more effective against adhesives by freezing them so they will chip off more easily.

Because of the above benefits dry ice is much more effective in specialized projects. When under time constraints dry ice is very beneficial because there is no clean up, the dry ice simply sublimates into a gaseous form and disappears.

blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.noWaste: No Secondary Waste - Dry ice sublimates directly into a gaseous state leaving no residue behind like the other blasting solutions.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.eco: Environmentally Friendly - Dry ice is created from reclaimed CO₂ and does not contribute to the greenhouse effect.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.nonConductive: Not Electrically Conductive - Dry ice can be used safely on live electrical systems.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.cold: Extreme Cold - Helps in removing adhesives, graffiti, and oils by freezing them.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.lessAbrasive: Less Abrasive - Won’t damage finishes or create grooves like other blasting methods.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.inPlace: Clean in Place - Portable equipment allows in-place cleaning, reducing downtime.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.foodSafe: Food Safe - Approved by EPA, FDA, USDA; kills bacteria and fungi without chemicals.
blasting_info.sections.benefits.text.fast: Faster and Safer - Cleans better than scrubbing and is more eco-friendly.

blasting_examples.title: Dry Ice Blasting Examples
blasting_examples.intro: Listed below are several examples of dry ice blasting on various surfaces. Blasting is quite loud and this is reflected in the videos, you may want to check your computer's volume before playing them all.
blasting_examples.examples.1.description: Dry Ice Blasting can be very gentle depending on the settings and type of ice you're using. In this example we're using the T2 dialed down so there's less air pressure, and because the T2 shaves ice off you get really fine grit instead of rice sized pellets (like a ColdJet, Wickens, Phoenix etc). The fine grit makes it so you don't have chunks taken out of your surface. With wood the grain pattern is more resistant, and the softer parts are removed first so you get an aged look. Dry Ice Blasting removes the top layer of wood, so deep stains from dyes, mould, or fire will not be completely removed.
